chunks: Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Isa, from Ibn Thabit, from Hanan, from Ibn Abi Yafur, from Isḥaq ibn ʿAmmār, from Abū ʿAbdillāh (peace be upon him), who said:

A mawlā (client) of ʿAlī (peace be upon him) died, so he said: 'Look, do you find an heir for him?' It was said to him: 'Two daughters in al-Yamāmah, who were enslaved.' So he purchased them with the wealth of the deceased mawlā, then handed over the remainder of the wealth to them.

key_terms.الْيَمَامَةِ: Al-Yamāmah, a historical region in Arabia
key_terms.مَمْلُوكَتَانِ: Two enslaved females, indicating their status as property but also as potential heirs
key_terms.مَوْلًى: Mawlā (client/freedman), a person who has been freed or has a patronage relationship
key_terms.وَارِثاً: Heir, one entitled to inherit the estate

ai.seo_question: How did Imam al-Sadiq handle the inheritance of a mawlā who had enslaved daughters as heirs?
ai.summary: This narration from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* illustrates the Imam’s practical application of inheritance law by purchasing the enslaved daughters of a mawlā to secure their status as heirs, thereby ensuring the estate's distribution aligns with Sharia. It highlights the scholarly principle that a mawlā’s lineage or acquired kinship can inherit alongside or in place of other relatives, emphasizing the Imam’s role in preserving the financial rights of freed clients. This case underscores the flexibility in determining heirship when direct male lineage is absent, focusing on the equitable transfer of wealth to female descendants.
